heroIntro: Entering into a contract for sale of immovable property (Bainapatra or Bayna Deed) is the standard preliminary step for buying land, commercial plots, or residential apartments in Bangladesh. Buyers frequently pay substantial advance earnest money—ranging from tens of lakhs to crores of BDT—trusting the seller to complete mutation, clear utility liens, and execute the final Saf Kabala transfer deed. However, due to rapid property appreciation, third-party broker meddling, or sheer bad faith, sellers often renege on the deal, refuse to accept the remaining balance, or secretly attempt to sell the property to a higher bidder. Under Section 12 and Section 21A of the Specific Relief Act 1877, a buyer is not helpless; the law empowers you to freeze the property and compel the civil court to execute the transfer on the defaulting seller's behalf.

quickAnswer.title: Can You Force a Seller to Register Land After Paying Bayna Advance in Bangladesh?
quickAnswer.text: Yes. Under Section 12 and Section 21A of the Specific Relief Act 1877, a purchaser can file a Suit for Specific Performance of Contract (Chukti Proborton Mamla) in the Joint District Judge Court to legally compel the seller to execute the final Saf Kabala deed. To enforce specific performance under Bangladeshi law, the Bayna Deed must be in writing and registered under the Registration Act 1908, and the buyer must deposit the entire remaining balance of consideration in court at the time of filing the plaint. The court can issue an immediate temporary injunction under Order 39 CPC restraining the seller from transferring the land to third parties, and upon decreeing the suit, the court registrar will sign and register the deed on the defaulting seller's behalf.
highlights: Section 21A makes registered Bayna deeds legally enforceable through civil courts.
The buyer must deposit the remaining balance of purchase money into the court treasury.
Courts issue immediate Order 39 temporary injunctions restraining third-party transfers.
If the seller refuses to comply with the decree, the court executes and registers the deed.
points: Governing Statutes: Specific Relief Act 1877 (Sections 12, 19, 21A) & Registration Act 1908 (Section 17A).
Limitation Period: 1 year from the date fixed for performance, or date of refusal (Article 113 Limitation Act).
Trial Forum: Joint District Judge Court having territorial jurisdiction over the property.

sections.title: 1. The Legal Framework: Mandatory Registration of Bayna Deeds (Section 17A)
sections.content:
Prior to 2004, contracts for the sale of land in Bangladesh were frequently executed on informal non-judicial stamp papers without official registration. Sellers exploited this informality by signing multiple unregistered Bayna deeds with different buyers, pocketing advances from all, and tying victims up in endless criminal or civil disputes.

To eliminate this predatory practice, parliament enacted sweeping amendments through the Registration (Amendment) Act 2004 and the Specific Relief (Amendment) Act 2004. Under Section 17A of the Registration Act 1908, a contract for the sale of any immovable property must be in writing, executed on prescribed non-judicial stamp paper, and presented for registration before the relevant Sub-Registry Office within thirty (30) days from execution.

Under Section 17A(2), an unregistered contract for sale has zero legal validity in respect of immovable property and cannot be received as evidence of any transaction affecting the land. Consequently, buyers must ensure that their Bayna deed is formally registered at the Sub-Registry Office; an informal notarized agreement cannot sustain a specific performance lawsuit.

sections.title: 2. Section 21A Prerequisites: Written Contract and Balance Court Deposit
sections.content:
The legal enforceability of a registered contract for sale is strictly governed by Section 21A of the Specific Relief Act 1877. This statutory provision establishes an affirmative right for the buyer while creating mandatory procedural prerequisites.

Under Section 21A, no suit for the specific performance of a contract for the sale of immovable property shall lie unless:

  • Registered Instrument: The contract is in writing and duly registered under the Registration Act 1908.
  • Mandatory Balance Deposit: The plaintiff deposits the remaining balance of the contract price in the civil court at the time of filing the plaint, or furnishes sufficient bank guarantee security if permitted by the court.

This statutory balance deposit requirement separates genuine purchasers from speculative litigants. By depositing the remaining consideration into the government treasury chalan, the buyer demonstrates absolute readiness and willingness to perform their contractual obligations, stripping the defaulting seller of any equitable defense.

sections.title: 3. Limitation Deadlines: The Strict One-Year Rule under Article 113
sections.content:
Time is of the essence when a land seller shows signs of default. Under Article 113 of the First Schedule to the Limitation Act 1908, the statutory limitation period for filing a suit for specific performance of a contract is strictly one (1) year.

The limitation clock begins running from one of two dates:

  1. Date Fixed for Performance: If the registered Bayna deed specifies a fixed date or timeframe for final deed registration (e.g., 'within six months from the date of execution'), the one-year limitation period begins running immediately upon the expiry of that specified date.
  2. Date of Refusal: If no fixed date was stipulated in the agreement, the limitation period begins running from the date when the plaintiff has formal notice that performance is refused by the seller.

sections.title: 4. Immediate Tactical Steps: Advocate Notice and Order 39 Injunction
sections.content:
The moment a seller begins making excuses—refusing to deliver mutation papers, demanding unauthorized extra money, or evading telephone calls—the buyer must establish a formal evidentiary paper trail.

The first mandatory procedural step is issuing a formal Legal Notice through an advocate via registered post with acknowledgment due (A/D). The notice must recite the registered Bayna deed particulars, specify that the buyer is ready with the remaining balance, propose a specific date, time, and Sub-Registry Office for final Saf Kabala execution, and warn that failure to attend will trigger immediate civil litigation.

Concurrently with filing the plaint in court, the buyer must file an emergency application for temporary injunction under Order 39, Rules 1 and 2 of the Code of Civil Procedure (CPC). The application requests the court to restrain the seller from transferring, mortgaging, selling, leasing, or altering the physical character of the property pending final disposal of the suit. Obtaining an interim injunction prevents the seller from creating third-party purchaser complications.

sections.title: 5. Filing the Suit for Specific Performance in the Joint District Judge Court
sections.content:
Because suits for specific performance of immovable property typically involve substantial pecuniary valuations, they fall under the original jurisdiction of the Joint District Judge Court having territorial authority over where the land is located.

The procedural journey encompasses:

  • Plaint Drafting & Court Fees: The plaint must set forth the complete transaction history, assert the plaintiff's continuous readiness and willingness, and attach the registered Bayna deed. The plaintiff pays the statutory ad valorem court fee under the Court Fees Act 1870 (capped at the statutory maximum).
  • Depositing the Treasury Chalan: The plaintiff deposits the remaining balance via treasury chalan, submitting the original receipt with the plaint.
  • Service of Summons: Summons are served on the defaulting seller under Order 5 CPC. If the seller evades service, summons are published in national daily newspapers.
  • Written Statement & Trial: The seller files a written statement (Jabab). The court frames issues, takes documentary and oral evidence, and hears final legal arguments.

sections.title: 6. Summary Matrix: Specific Performance vs. Refund of Advance with Penalty
sections.content:
A purchaser facing seller breach must evaluate whether to pursue compulsory land registration or demand a financial refund with contractual penalties. The following matrix outlines the strategic distinctions:

Remedy Pathway Governing Statute Prerequisites & Deposits Ultimate Relief Obtained
Specific Performance of Contract Specific Relief Act 1877 (Sec 12, 21A) Registered Bayna deed; mandatory deposit of balance consideration Court executes and registers final Saf Kabala deed to buyer
Refund of Advance with Penalty / Compensation Specific Relief Act 1877 (Sec 19) / Contract Act (Sec 73) No balance deposit required; proof of advance payment vouchers Money decree for double the advance or damages plus interest
Criminal Cheating Prosecution The Penal Code 1860 (Sec 406, 420) Proof of fraudulent dishonest inducement at inception Criminal conviction/fine; does not transfer land title directly
Temporary Injunction / Status Quo Code of Civil Procedure (Order 39) Prima facie case, irreparable loss, balance of convenience Freezes property, preventing third-party sale or construction

sections.title: 7. Execution of Decree: How the Civil Court Registers the Deed for You
sections.content:
A common concern among buyers is: 'What if the court passes a decree, but the stubborn seller still refuses to go to the Sub-Registry Office?' The civil procedure code provides a foolproof enforcement mechanism.

When the Joint District Judge decrees the suit for specific performance, the judgment grants the seller a fixed period (typically 30 to 60 days) to appear at the Sub-Registry Office, accept the deposited balance from the court, and execute the Saf Kabala deed. If the seller willfully fails or refuses to appear within the stipulated period, the decree-holder files a Title Execution Case (Jari Mamla) under Order 21, Rule 34 of the CPC.

Under Order 21, Rule 34, the civil court itself steps into the shoes of the defaulting seller. The presiding judge drafts the deed, delivers notice to the Sub-Registrar, and authorizes the Court Nazir or Sheristadar to attend the Sub-Registry Office. The court officer signs and presents the deed for registration on behalf of the judgment-debtor. The resulting registered deed carries absolute, incontestable statutory validity under Bangladeshi property law.

sections.title: 8. Illustrative Scenario: Buyer Compelling Registration Against an Unruly Seller
sections.content:
To illustrate how specific performance litigation operates in practice, consider the following illustrative scenario (composite; names and details changed).

A software executive in Uttara, Dhaka, agreed to purchase a 5-katha residential plot in Bashundhara for 1.2 Crore BDT. The parties executed a registered Bayna Deed under Section 17A of the Registration Act, with the buyer paying 40 Lakh BDT as advance earnest money, and stipulating a four-month timeframe to complete the remaining 80 Lakh BDT upon delivery of municipal mutation papers. Within three months, land values in the sector surged by 25%.

The seller abruptly stopped answering phone calls, refused to provide the mutation porcha, and engaged local brokers to sell the plot to a third party for 1.5 Crore BDT. The buyer retained a Supreme Court land advocate. The advocate immediately issued a formal statutory legal notice demanding registration, followed by filing a Suit for Specific Performance before the Joint District Judge Court, Dhaka, under Section 21A.

The buyer deposited the remaining 80 Lakh BDT into the government treasury chalan on the day of filing. Concurrently, the advocate moved an Order 39 injunction petition, and the court issued an immediate order restraining the seller from transferring or encumbering the land. Confronted with the frozen land title and the deposited court balance, the seller realized evading the transaction was legally impossible and appeared before the court to execute the final Saf Kabala deed.

sections.title: 9. Essential Due Diligence Checklist for Buyers Before Signing Bayna Deeds
sections.content:
Protecting your financial investment begins before a single BDT changes hands. Follow this mandatory due diligence protocol prior to executing any land agreement in Bangladesh:

  • Demand Registered Bayna Only: Never settle for an unregistered agreement or notary public stamp. Insist that the Bayna deed is formally registered at the local Sub-Registry Office.
  • Verify CS, SA, RS, and BS Khatians: Confirm that the seller's name or immediate predecessor's name is recorded in the latest BS/City Jarip Khatian and that the chain of title is unbroken.
  • Check Mutation & Up-to-Date Khajna: Verify that the land has been mutated (Namjari) in the seller's name by the relevant AC Land and that Land Development Tax receipts (Dakhila) are cleared for the current fiscal year.
  • Stipulate Clear Handover Deadlines: Explicitly state the final date for deed execution, consequences of seller default, and a clause specifying that the buyer reserves the right to seek specific performance under Section 21A.
  • Pay Advances Through Banking Channels: Never pay Bayna advances in unrecorded cash. Utilize account-payee cheques, pay orders, or RTGS bank transfers with clear payment reference memos.

faqs.question: Can I force a seller to register land if they refuse after taking Bayna in Bangladesh?
faqs.answer: Yes. If you have a registered Bayna Deed, you can file a Suit for Specific Performance of Contract under Section 21A of the Specific Relief Act 1877 to compel the seller to execute the deed, or have the court register it on their behalf.

faqs.question: Is an unregistered Bayna deed legally enforceable in court?
faqs.answer: No. Under Section 17A of the Registration Act 1908 and Section 21A of the Specific Relief Act 1877, an unregistered contract for sale of immovable property cannot sustain a suit for specific performance.

faqs.question: Do I have to deposit the remaining land price in court when filing the suit?
faqs.answer: Yes. Section 21A of the Specific Relief Act makes it mandatory for the purchaser to deposit the remaining balance of consideration in court at the time of filing the plaint, demonstrating absolute readiness and willingness.

faqs.question: What is the limitation period to file a suit for specific performance in Bangladesh?
faqs.answer: Under Article 113 of the Limitation Act 1908, the lawsuit must be filed within one (1) year from the date fixed for performance, or from the date when the seller formally refused performance.

faqs.question: How can I stop the seller from selling the land to someone else during the lawsuit?
faqs.answer: You must file an application for temporary injunction under Order 39, Rules 1 and 2 of the Code of Civil Procedure (CPC) to restrain the seller from transferring, mortgaging, or altering the land pending final decree.

faqs.question: What happens if the court decrees specific performance but the seller refuses to sign?
faqs.answer: Under Order 21, Rule 34 of the CPC, the civil court itself executes and registers the Saf Kabala deed on behalf of the defaulting seller through a court-appointed officer, granting the buyer full legal ownership.

faqs.question: Can I claim double the advance money back instead of the land?
faqs.answer: Yes. Under Section 19 of the Specific Relief Act and contractual terms, a buyer can plead in the alternative for compensation, demanding a refund of the earnest money alongside agreed penalty damages.

faqs.question: Can an overseas Bangladeshi buyer file a specific performance suit from abroad?
faqs.answer: Yes. An overseas Bangladeshi can execute a Special Power of Attorney attested by the Bangladesh Embassy or High Commission, authorizing a lawyer or relative to deposit the balance and conduct the lawsuit in Bangladesh.
